modalities.name: What Holds You Now
modalities.tagline: Deep, steady attention on the real support under your body.
modalities.whatItIs: What Holds You Now is a proposed concentration practice whose only object is the actual feeling of being supported: the seat under you, the floor under your feet and the backrest behind you. It keeps the steady, deepening focus of absorption meditation but uses nothing imagined, no remembered people and no guide, so you can learn it from a printed card and practice alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Steadiness does not have to come from an imagined or remembered figure: the chair and the floor are holding you right now, and resting attention on that plain fact, again and again, is meant to build a calm, absorbed focus out of real contact.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit on a firm chair for 20 minutes with feet flat and eyes closed or lowered, and follow the four steps on the card: feel where the seat presses, where the feet press, where the back is supported, and then all three contact areas at once. Whenever an image, a memory or a story appears, let it go without following it and return to the pressure and weight that are actually there. As attention steadies, let the whole feeling of support become the single thing you attend to, and end with a minute of opening your eyes and looking around the room.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find guided imagery or inner figures hard or unwelcome and want a calming focus they can check against what is really there, and anyone who wants a simple, self-taught way into deeper concentration.
modalities.cautions: Long or intensive concentration sits can bring strong sensations, altered perception or fear, so keep sessions short at first and seek out a teacher experienced with meditation-related difficulties if anything unsettling persists. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician before practicing; it is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Nothing imagined, nobody to picture. An idea for a calming practice: 20 minutes resting your attention on the chair and floor that are actually holding you up, until that plain feeling of support is all you notice. Learnable from a card.

modalities.name: One Undivided Body
modalities.tagline: Feel the whole body at once, as one undivided sensation.
modalities.whatItIs: One Undivided Body is a proposed absorption practice in which you sense the entire body at once, as a single field of sensation, instead of attending to any one part of it or to any inner voice. It follows a fixed sequence that you learn from a short course or recording and then practice alone, and it stays entirely with the present.
modalities.coreIdea: Many approaches divide inner life into parts, voices or regions; this one goes the other way, gathering all of attention into one whole, so that the felt sense of being one undivided body becomes the steady object of concentration.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sitting still for 25 minutes, you begin with five minutes on the breath, then widen attention in set stages: the torso as one shape, then torso and head, then the whole body including hands and feet, felt all at once. Whenever attention narrows to one spot, such as an itch, or splits off into an inner conversation, you notice it and widen back out to the whole. For the last ten minutes you simply stay with the whole-body field as one steady sensation, then open your eyes slowly.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel scattered or pulled in many directions inside and want a structured way to feel collected and whole, without any talk about inner parts.
modalities.cautions: Widening into a whole-body sense can sometimes feel strange, floaty or unreal, so open your eyes and feel your feet on the floor if it does, and stop if it keeps happening. Learn with a teacher experienced in meditation-related difficulties, and anyone with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should check with a clinician first; this is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: What if you felt your whole body at once, as one single sensation, instead of zooming in on its parts? A new concept: a 25-minute sit that widens attention in set stages until the body feels like one steady whole. Might suit anyone who feels scattered.

modalities.name: Wordless Warmth
modalities.tagline: Rest in the warmth under your hands, with no words at all.
modalities.whatItIs: Wordless Warmth is a proposed lying-down concentration practice built on one bodily feeling: the mild warmth where your hands rest on your belly. It drops every kind of thinking work, such as labeling, weighing evidence or judging how it is going, and lets a calm, pleasant feeling in the body become the whole object.
modalities.coreIdea: Thinking about how you feel can keep the mind busy and switched on, so this practice gives the mind nothing to analyze and lets a simple, physical sense of ease do the steadying instead.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lie on your back on a mat or bed for 20 minutes, rub your palms together for a few seconds and rest them on your belly, then let attention settle where the warmth and the gentle rise of the hands are felt. When a thought starts to comment, compare or check progress, let it go without answering it and come back to the warmth, and if the warmth fades, rest in whatever ease remains in the belly. You learn the method from a teacher or a recording and then use it on your own, often in the evening.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose minds keep analyzing and checking, even while relaxing, and who want a soft, body-based way into deep calm.
modalities.cautions: Strong pleasant states can be followed by flatness or restlessness, and researchers have asked whether chasing such feelings could turn into craving, so keep the aim gentle and the sessions modest. Deep calm practice can also bring up difficult experiences, so learn with a teacher who knows about them, and check with a clinician first if you have a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation; it is untested.
modalities.tweet: Picture this: lying down, warm palms resting on your belly, no labels and no analysis, just the warmth and the slow rise of breath under your hands. Wordless Warmth is an untested idea for minds that keep checking, even while trying to relax.

modalities.name: The Unvarying Sit
modalities.tagline: Same seat, same time, same object, every day for eight weeks.
modalities.whatItIs: The Unvarying Sit is a proposed concentration practice in which nothing is allowed to change: the place, the time, the posture, the length and the object of attention stay exactly the same for eight weeks. Where many approaches prize flexibility and variety, this one bets on total sameness as a way to build a deeply steady, absorbed attention.
modalities.coreIdea: Doing exactly the same sit in exactly the same setting, day after day, is meant to turn the setting itself into a cue, so that sitting down in that seat at that hour may come to bring steady attention almost by itself.
modalities.whatYouDo: With a teacher you choose once, at the start, a seat, a time of day, a session length of 20 or 30 minutes and one object, such as the rise and fall of the belly, and write them on a card. Every day you sit at that time in that seat and rest attention only on that object, coming back to it whenever it slips, and you make no adjustments, even on days that feel dull or restless. You mark each day's sit with a single tick, and the teacher checks in every two weeks.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who tinker endlessly with their practice or their apps and want to find out what steady repetition alone might do.
modalities.cautions: Rigid daily concentration can feel grinding, and deep sits can bring up strange or frightening experiences, so it is fine to shorten or stop a session and to talk it over with a teacher experienced in meditation-related difficulties. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician first; this concept is untested.
modalities.tweet: Eight weeks, zero changes. Same chair, same time, same object of attention, every single day. The Unvarying Sit is a new idea that tests whether total sameness, rather than variety, might let your focus settle deeper. Fine to stop any day.

modalities.name: Toward the Finest Breath
modalities.tagline: Let each breath grow a little quieter until it is barely there.
modalities.whatItIs: Toward the Finest Breath is a proposed calming practice in which the breath is allowed, never forced, to become finer, smoother and quieter over a sit, and that ever subtler breath becomes the object of concentration. It looks for nothing underneath experience and asks for no insight: settling is the whole aim, and after a few lessons you can practice it alone.
modalities.coreIdea: As the body settles, breathing tends to become lighter, and following that lightening closely is meant to draw attention into a deep, quiet steadiness without any need to discover or understand anything.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sit or recline for 20 minutes and spend the first five simply feeling the breath at the belly and nostrils. In three set stages of five minutes, you invite each breath to be a little softer and quieter than the last, the way you might lower your voice in a sleeping house, while letting the body take as much air as it wants. In the final stage you stay with whatever fine thread of breath remains, and if you feel short of air, you take a few full, normal breaths and carry on.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel wound up and want the most settling form of concentration, without any digging into feelings or reasons.
modalities.cautions: Trying to make the breath smaller can cause air hunger, dizziness or anxiety, so never hold or restrict the breath, breathe normally whenever you want to, and check with a doctor first if you have breathing or heart problems or panic attacks. Deep calm sits can also bring up difficult experiences, so learn with a teacher experienced in them, and talk to a clinician first if you have a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation; it is untested.
modalities.tweet: A new concept for wound-up nervous systems: sit for 20 minutes and let each breath become a little quieter than the last, never forced, until only a fine thread is left to follow. If you feel short of air, you simply breathe normally.

modalities.name: The Windless Flame
modalities.tagline: Hold an imagined flame so still that it never flickers.
modalities.whatItIs: The Windless Flame is a proposed concentration practice in which the body stays completely still and the mind holds one imagined picture: a candle flame in a room with no draft. It moves away from body-led practices that let the muscles tremble or shake, toward the steadiest, most deliberate kind of inner stillness, and it is learned in a small, silent class.
modalities.coreIdea: A flame that does not flicker gives the mind a clear picture of steadiness to match, and keeping that picture steady is meant to train a calm, unwavering attention with the body left out of it.
modalities.whatYouDo: After the teacher introduces the image, you sit upright and motionless for 20 minutes with eyes closed and picture a small flame in a still room, keeping the picture simple. Whenever the flame wavers, grows, changes color or turns into something else, you let it settle back into the same still flame without forcing it, and if no picture comes, you hold the idea of the flame instead. The class meets weekly for six weeks, and between classes you practice once a day at home.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who think in pictures and want a quiet, mental anchor, including those who prefer a practice that asks nothing of the body.
modalities.cautions: Imagined pictures can sometimes become vivid, change on their own or feel unsettling, so open your eyes and look around the room if that happens and tell the teacher, who should be experienced with meditation-related difficulties. Anyone with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician before starting; it is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Imagine a candle flame in a room with no draft at all, and hold that picture so still it never flickers, while your body stays still too. The Windless Flame: an untested idea for a quiet, picture-based way to steady a restless mind.

modalities.name: Place, Hold, Release
modalities.tagline: Timed drills that train you to aim attention and keep it there.
modalities.whatItIs: Place, Hold, Release is a proposed attention-training class built on the two skills that open the way into absorption meditation: directing attention to an object and keeping it there. Instead of waiting for something to emerge or listening for what a feeling means, you practice aiming and holding attention on purpose, in timed drills called by a teacher.
modalities.coreIdea: Placing attention and keeping it in place may be learnable like any other skill, through short, repeated drills with clear feedback, without asking what anything means.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a weekly 45-minute class of a few people sitting in silence, the teacher calls out a small spot, such as the tip of the nose, the center of the left palm or the top of the head, and you place attention there and hold it until the next call, which comes after 30 seconds at first and after up to five minutes by the end of the course. At each 'release' you let attention go wide for a few breaths and silently count how many times it slipped. You repeat a shorter set at home each day and tell the teacher how the counts change.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who like learning by drills and want a clear, practical way to train concentration before trying longer meditation.
modalities.cautions: Hard, effortful focus can bring headaches, tension or fatigue, and long concentration practice can bring up unsettling experiences, so keep the effort moderate and have a teacher experienced with meditation-related difficulties. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician first; it is a new, untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Concentration as a trainable skill: a teacher calls a spot, like the center of your palm, and you aim attention there and hold it until the next call, building from 30 seconds to 5 minutes. Place, Hold, Release is an untested class idea.

modalities.name: Steadiness Ladder
modalities.tagline: A self-run course of concentration milestones, one rung at a time.
modalities.whatItIs: Steadiness Ladder is a proposed self-guided course in concentration made of fixed steps, each with a clear test you pass before moving to the next. Rather than an open, coach-led conversation that follows whatever is present, it is a set program you run and score yourself, aimed at building steady attention on one object.
modalities.coreIdea: Clear milestones and simple self-tests may turn the vague goal of getting better at concentrating into a series of definite, reachable steps.
modalities.whatYouDo: You choose one object, such as the breath at the nostrils, sit daily for 20 minutes and work through a printed ladder of eight rungs, for example: count ten breaths without losing track, then twenty, then stay with the object for one minute without a lapse, then five minutes. You test yourself at the end of each sit and tick a rung only after passing it on three days in a row, never skipping one. If you stall on a rung for two weeks, you step down one rung for a week before trying again.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who stay motivated by clear goals and progress charts and want a do-it-yourself path into deeper concentration.
modalities.cautions: Scoring your own meditation can breed frustration or striving, so it is fine to step down or pause, and deeper concentration can bring strong, unusual or frightening experiences that call for a teacher experienced in meditation-related difficulties. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician first; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Count ten breaths without losing track. Then twenty. Then one unbroken minute on one object, then five. Steadiness Ladder is a new do-it-yourself idea: eight rungs, and you climb only after passing a rung three days in a row.

modalities.name: Intention Every Breath
modalities.tagline: Renew the choice to attend before every single breath.
modalities.whatItIs: Intention Every Breath is a proposed, tightly structured concentration practice in which you renew a deliberate intention to attend before each breath, so nothing about where attention goes is left to drift. It is the furthest possible step from practices that drop all control: every moment is chosen, and a teacher sets the exact form and checks it with you.
modalities.coreIdea: Attention usually wanders in the gaps where no one is steering, so filling every gap with a fresh, quiet decision to stay is meant to train the firmest possible hold over where attention rests.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a small silent group led by a teacher, you sit for 20 minutes and, in the pause before each in-breath, silently form one short intention, such as 'this breath', then follow that breath from its start to its end at the belly. If you notice that a breath went by without an intention, you simply renew it at the next pause, with no scolding. After the sit the teacher asks each person how often the intention was lost and adjusts the length of the next week's sits.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who drift off whenever they meditate and want the most structured, deliberate form of concentration, with a teacher alongside.
modalities.cautions: Such tight control can bring tension, headaches or anxious striving, so keep the intention light, and very focused practice can bring up unusual or distressing experiences that need a teacher experienced in meditation-related difficulties. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should check with a clinician first; it is untested.
modalities.tweet: Before every in-breath, one silent decision: 'this breath'. Then you follow it to its end and choose again. A new concept for chronic drifters: meditation where no moment is left unsteered, practiced in a small group with a teacher.

modalities.name: Neutral Touch Point
modalities.tagline: Steady attention on a touch that is neither pleasant nor unpleasant.
modalities.whatItIs: Neutral Touch Point is a proposed concentration practice whose object is deliberately plain: the light touch of thumb against index fingertip, a sensation with no person, no warmth and no wish attached. It aims for a cool, even calm rather than a warm or loving feeling, and a teacher introduces it in a short course before you practice alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Calm does not need to be warm or emotional: a sensation that is neither pleasant nor unpleasant gives attention nothing to want or push away, which is meant to let a cool, even steadiness grow.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sitting still for 20 minutes, you rest one hand on your thigh with the thumb lightly touching the tip of the index finger, and keep attention on that small point of contact: its pressure, temperature and faint pulse. When feelings, wishes or thoughts of people arise, you let them pass and return to the plain contact, and if the touch starts to feel pleasant or uncomfortable, you note that and keep attending to the touch itself. The course has four weekly sessions in which the teacher answers questions, and afterwards you practice daily at home.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find warm, heart-centered practices uncomfortable or too emotional, and anyone who wants a cool, even form of calm.
modalities.cautions: Steady concentration can sometimes bring numbness, strange sensations or fear rather than calm, so stop if that happens and talk it over with a teacher experienced in meditation-related difficulties. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician before practicing; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Not every calm has to feel warm and loving. An idea: 20 minutes resting attention on the plain touch of thumb against fingertip, a sensation that is neither nice nor nasty, so there is nothing to want or push away. A teacher shows you first.

modalities.name: The Unbroken Line
modalities.tagline: Draw one imagined line and keep it from breaking.
modalities.whatItIs: The Unbroken Line is a proposed concentration practice in which you picture a single line being drawn slowly across an inner page and keep it continuous for as long as you can. It works in the opposite direction from insight practices that break experience into passing moments: the aim is one seamless thread of attention, taught in a short class and then practiced daily.
modalities.coreIdea: Insight meditation watches experience split into countless separate moments; this practice deliberately joins attention into one continuous stream, using the picture of a line that must not break.
modalities.whatYouDo: With eyes closed, you picture a fine line starting at the left of an inner page and extending slowly to the right, at about the speed of an unhurried pen, and when it reaches the edge it simply carries on along a new row, like writing without letters. When attention lapses and the line breaks, you notice the gap without studying it and start drawing again from the point where it broke. Sits last 20 minutes, and the teacher checks in weekly on how long the line tends to stay unbroken.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find watching every changing moment tiring or fragmenting and want a smooth, continuous kind of focus.
modalities.cautions: Mental pictures can sometimes turn vivid or unsettling, so open your eyes if that happens, keep sessions moderate and have a teacher experienced with meditation-related difficulties on hand. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician before starting; it has no track record.
modalities.tweet: Draw a line in your mind and never let it break. If it snaps, you pick it up exactly where it broke and keep going, for 20 quiet minutes. The Unbroken Line is a new concept for minds that feel chopped into a thousand little bits.

modalities.name: When the Swing Stops
modalities.tagline: Picture a swing slowing down, then rest in its stillness.
modalities.whatItIs: When the Swing Stops is a proposed lying-down practice in which you picture an empty playground swing slowly coming to a stop, then rest attention on its stillness. It is the furthest thing from bursts of hard effort: no movement, no counting and no push, only a picture of motion winding down, learned from a teacher and then used alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Following an imagined movement as it slows to a halt may invite the mind to wind down with it, and the stillness at the end then becomes the object of quiet, steady attention.
modalities.whatYouDo: Lying on your back with eyes closed, you picture a swing moving in wide arcs, then let each arc become shorter and slower over a few minutes until the swing hangs still. You rest attention on the still swing for as long as it stays clear, and when the mind starts racing again, you let the swing begin a small, gentle arc and slow it to rest once more. A session lasts about 20 minutes, after a short teacher-led introduction, with a check-in once a month.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel revved up and find sitting with the breath too demanding, and who want an easy, picture-based way to slow down.
modalities.cautions: Lying still with eyes closed can lead to sleep, which is harmless, but imagery practice can occasionally bring up unsettling pictures or feelings, so open your eyes if it does and see a teacher experienced in meditation-related difficulties if it keeps happening. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician first; this concept is untested.
modalities.tweet: An idea for revved-up evenings: lie back, picture an empty swing moving in wide arcs, and let it slow down, arc by arc, until it hangs still. Then just rest your attention on that stillness. No effort, no counting, about 20 minutes.

modalities.name: Down to a Pinpoint
modalities.tagline: Shrink an imagined circle, stage by stage, to a single point.
modalities.whatItIs: Down to a Pinpoint is a proposed solitary concentration practice in which you picture a circle and narrow it in set stages until only a single point remains, then rest there. It is the opposite of tracking many people and moving things at once: alone, still and quiet, with one ever smaller object, following a teacher's instructions.
modalities.coreIdea: Attention may steady most easily when it has less and less to hold, so narrowing one imagined shape step by step is meant to gather a scattered mind into the smallest possible object.
modalities.whatYouDo: Sitting alone in a quiet room, you follow the teacher's recorded instructions to picture a circle the size of a dinner plate and then, every four minutes, a smaller one: a saucer, a coin, a pea and finally a single point. You stay with the point for the last ten minutes, and if it blurs or vanishes, you go back to the coin and narrow again. You meet the teacher every two weeks to talk through what happened and decide whether to lengthen the final stage.
modalities.whoItsFor: People whose days are full of other people and fast demands, and who want a solitary practice that narrows everything down to one point.
modalities.cautions: Very narrow focus can bring tension, headaches or odd visual effects, and deep solitary concentration can bring up frightening experiences, so stop if it feels wrong and stay in touch with a teacher experienced in meditation-related difficulties. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician first; it is untested.
modalities.tweet: Plate, saucer, coin, pea, point. A new solitary practice: alone in a quiet room, you picture a circle and shrink it in stages until only a pinpoint is left, then rest your attention there. Might suit people whose days are full of noise and other people.

modalities.name: Resting in Enough
modalities.tagline: A guided practice of settling into the feeling of enough.
modalities.whatItIs: Resting in Enough is a proposed teacher-led practice that takes contentment, one of the qualities described in absorption meditation, as the object of concentration. Instead of pushing on through effort and distance, you call up the plain feeling of 'that's enough', settle into it and stay there, following a fixed script that a teacher reads in every session.
modalities.coreIdea: Many people know how to keep going but rarely notice the moment of having enough, and dwelling in that feeling on purpose is meant to make it familiar and steady and to give the mind a quiet place to rest.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a seated 30-minute session, the teacher reads the same script each week: first you settle with a few breaths, then you call up a recent, ordinary moment of having enough, such as putting down an empty plate after a good meal or sitting down at the end of a walk. As soon as the feeling of enough is there, you let the scene go and rest attention on the feeling alone, returning to the scene briefly only if the feeling fades. The session ends with a few minutes of quiet and one sentence to the teacher about what the feeling was like.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who always push for more and find it hard to stop, and who want a gentle, guided way to practice feeling satisfied.
modalities.cautions: Use only recent, everyday moments, not old or painful memories, and if a scene brings up sadness or anything difficult, open your eyes and tell the teacher, who should be experienced in meditation-related difficulties. Anyone with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician first; it is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: What if you practiced the feeling of 'that's enough' the way runners practice going further? A new, teacher-led idea: recall a small, recent moment of having enough, like an empty plate after a good meal, then let the scene go and rest in the feeling.

modalities.name: Holding a Soap Bubble
modalities.tagline: Keep attention on an imagined bubble without gripping it.
modalities.whatItIs: Holding a Soap Bubble is a proposed concentration practice built around the lightest possible effort: you hold an imagined soap bubble in attention, firmly enough to keep it and gently enough not to burst it. It runs the other way from practices built on pushing against a load, and a teacher introduces it before you practice alone.
modalities.coreIdea: Concentration can fail by gripping too hard as well as by letting go, and a fragile imagined object gives quick, gentle feedback about which one is happening.
modalities.whatYouDo: Seated comfortably for 15 to 20 minutes, you picture a soap bubble resting in your open palms and keep attention on it lightly. If you catch yourself straining, frowning or holding the breath, you imagine the bubble bursting, let a new one appear and soften your effort, and if your mind wanders off, you imagine the bubble drifting away and bring a new one back. Over a few weeks the teacher helps you notice what kind of effort keeps the bubble longest.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who try too hard at everything, including relaxing, and want to feel what gentle effort is like.
modalities.cautions: Mental pictures can sometimes become vivid or unsettling, and deeper concentration can bring strong or frightening experiences, so open your eyes if needed and learn with a teacher experienced in meditation-related difficulties. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should check with a clinician first; this is a new, untested idea.
modalities.tweet: Grip too hard and it bursts. Let go and it drifts away. A new idea for chronic over-triers: hold an imagined soap bubble in your attention for 15 minutes, using exactly as much effort as it takes to keep it, and not an ounce more.

modalities.name: Your Own Inner Emblem
modalities.tagline: Design a simple symbol in your mind and make it your focus.
modalities.whatItIs: Your Own Inner Emblem is a proposed self-led concentration practice whose object is a simple symbol you design yourself, describe in one written line and then rebuild in your mind's eye each day. Nothing about it is alive, responsive or unpredictable: it is a still, private object of your own making, practiced alone with a short written guide.
modalities.coreIdea: An object you made yourself stays exactly as you made it and asks nothing of you, which may make it an especially steady and personal place for attention to rest.
modalities.whatYouDo: On the first day you imagine a plain symbol of two or three strokes, such as a small gray circle crossed by one upright line, and write a one-line description of it in a notebook. Each day after that you sit for 20 minutes with eyes closed, rebuild the emblem from that description and hold it, letting go of any changes, colors or extra details that creep in, and rereading the line only if the picture fades completely. You keep the same emblem for at least two months before changing anything.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who prefer to practice alone, without a teacher, an animal or anyone else, and who like a personal object they shaped themselves.
modalities.cautions: Mental pictures can occasionally turn vivid, change on their own or feel unsettling, so open your eyes and stop if that happens, and talk any strong experience through with a teacher experienced in meditation-related difficulties. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician before starting; it is untested.
modalities.tweet: Design a simple symbol in your mind, write one line describing it, and from then on that is your object of focus, rebuilt from memory each day for 20 quiet minutes. Your Own Inner Emblem: an untested idea, made to be practiced entirely on your own.

modalities.name: Off-Beat Counting
modalities.tagline: A slow inner count that never follows the breath.
modalities.whatItIs: Off-Beat Counting is a proposed concentration practice in which the object is a slow, silent count that runs at its own even pace, deliberately out of step with the breath and with no movement at all. Where body-based practices tie the mind to breathing and posture, this one cuts that tie and lets attention rest on a purely mental rhythm.
modalities.coreIdea: Freeing attention from the breath may show that the mind can hold a steady object of its own, and a plain count is about as simple and neutral as such an object can be.
modalities.whatYouDo: After learning the method from a teacher, you sit still for 20 minutes and count silently from one to ten at an even pace of roughly one number every three seconds, then start again at one, letting the breath do whatever it does. If you notice the count slipping into step with the breath or speeding up, you leave the breath alone and return to the even pace, and if you lose the count, you begin again at one without judging it. Once a month you check in with the teacher about how steady the count has become.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find that focusing on the breath makes them tense or self-conscious, and who want a calm, simple mental object instead.
modalities.cautions: Repetitive counting can become dull or tense, so keep the pace easy, and long concentration practice can bring up unusual or distressing experiences that call for a teacher experienced with meditation-related difficulties. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician first; it is an untested concept.
modalities.tweet: Breath-focused meditation makes some people tense. So here is a new idea: count silently from one to ten at an even pace, about one number every three seconds, deliberately out of step with your breath, and let that steady count be the whole focus.

modalities.name: Speech at Rest
modalities.tagline: Bring every part of speaking to rest, outside and in.
modalities.whatItIs: Speech at Rest is a proposed teacher-led practice that brings the whole machinery of speech to rest, from the lips, tongue, jaw and throat to the silent rehearsing of conversations. It is done in silence, in a fixed sequence, and its aim is a deep calm in which there is nothing to say and no one to answer.
modalities.coreIdea: A lot of everyday tension seems to live in the muscles of speaking and in imagined conversations, so letting both go quiet, step by step, is meant to settle body and mind into a still, wordless calm.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a silent class, the teacher guides you in a set order to let the lips rest together, the tongue lie soft in the mouth, the jaw hang slightly loose and the throat soften, spending three minutes on each with eyes closed. Then, for ten minutes, whenever you catch yourself replaying or rehearsing a conversation, you let the imagined words fade before they finish and return to the quiet mouth and throat. The sit ends with five minutes of silence before anyone speaks, and you practice the same sequence alone at home with the teacher's recording.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who talk all day for work or keep replaying conversations in their heads, and who want a calm that starts in the mouth and throat.
modalities.cautions: Close attention to the throat or to swallowing can make some people anxious, so open your eyes and breathe normally if that happens, and deep calm practice can bring up difficult experiences that call for a teacher experienced in meditation-related difficulties. Anyone with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should check with a clinician first; this concept is untested.
modalities.tweet: Lips resting together, tongue soft, jaw loose, throat easy, and every rehearsed conversation allowed to fade mid-sentence. Speech at Rest is a new concept for anyone who talks all day: a guided, silent sit that quiets speaking from the outside in.

modalities.name: Bare Room Within
modalities.tagline: Build the same bare imagined room, piece by piece, every time.
modalities.whatItIs: Bare Room Within is a proposed teacher-led imagery practice in which you construct one plain, enclosed room in your mind, always in the same order and with the same few features, and then rest your attention inside it. It is the reverse of a walk outdoors: indoors instead of open, made instead of wild, and identical every time instead of always changing.
modalities.coreIdea: Unlike a personal comfort scene, the room is bare and the same for everyone, and a place that is deliberately built and never changes is meant to give attention a dependable, quiet setting to settle in.
modalities.whatYouDo: In weekly guided sessions, the teacher leads you through the same build in the same order: a plain wooden floor, four pale walls, one closed door, soft light from above and a single cushion in the middle. Once the room is complete, you imagine sitting on the cushion and rest attention on the quiet of the room for 15 minutes, rebuilding any part that fades. Between sessions you practice with the teacher's recording, never adding features or changing the room.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who find open, changing surroundings distracting and who like a fixed, step-by-step routine with a guide.
modalities.cautions: An enclosed imagined space can feel confining for some people, so it is fine to picture the door open or to stop, and imagery can occasionally become vivid or unsettling, which calls for a teacher experienced with meditation-related difficulties. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician first; it is untested.
modalities.tweet: The opposite of a wild walk in the hills: a guide helps you build the same bare imagined room, in the same order, every single time, and then you rest in its quiet for 15 minutes. A new concept for minds that like a fixed routine.

modalities.name: Doors Closing Inward
modalities.tagline: A guided sequence that withdraws attention from each sense in turn.
modalities.whatItIs: Doors Closing Inward is a proposed teacher-led practice in which attention is drawn back from the senses one at a time, sight, then sound, then touch, smell and taste, until it rests on a single quiet inner object. It turns away from attending to sights and sounds and toward the inward, secluded focus described in absorption meditation, following a fixed sequence.
modalities.coreIdea: Letting go of the senses deliberately and in a set order may make the move from outer noise to inner quiet gentler and more predictable than waiting for it to happen.
modalities.whatYouDo: In a small silent class, the teacher guides a 30-minute sit: for about four minutes per sense you notice it, then imagine a door gently closing on it and let it fade into the background, starting with sight and ending with taste. With the doors closed you rest attention on a simple inner object, such as the silent word 'still' or a soft inner glow, for the last ten minutes. At the end the teacher has you reopen each door in reverse order, opening your eyes last, and look around the room before standing up.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who feel overwhelmed by noise, screens and constant input, and who want a guided, step-by-step way to turn inward.
modalities.cautions: Turning away from the senses can feel disorienting or unreal for some people, so reopen them slowly at the end and stop if you feel detached afterward, and the class should be led by a teacher experienced with meditation-related difficulties. People with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician first; this is an untested idea.
modalities.tweet: One sense at a time, a teacher helps you close a door on sight, sound, touch, smell and taste, rest in the quiet behind them, then open each one again. Doors Closing Inward is an untested idea for anyone worn out by constant noise and screens.

modalities.name: One Note, No Song
modalities.tagline: Hold one imagined, unchanging note, with no melody or beat.
modalities.whatItIs: One Note, No Song is a proposed concentration practice that strips music down to a single imagined tone, held steady with no melody, rhythm, words or company. You hear the note only in your mind, feel it as a faint inner hum in the chest, and keep it the same from start to finish, following a fixed routine learned from a teacher.
modalities.coreIdea: Music moves feelings by changing, so one note that never changes is meant to give attention something calm and constant to rest on, without the pull of a tune.
modalities.whatYouDo: At your first lesson the teacher plays one low, steady tone for a minute so you can remember it, and after that you practice alone in silence. You sit for 20 minutes, call up the note in your mind and keep it at the same pitch and loudness, feeling it as if it were humming quietly in your chest without making any sound. When a tune, a rhythm or a different note sneaks in, you let it go and return to the one note, and if the note vanishes, you simply call it up again.
modalities.whoItsFor: People who love sound and find silent breath practice too dry, and who want a steady, musical-feeling anchor with no performing involved.
modalities.cautions: Imagined sounds can sometimes become loud, persistent or hard to stop, so end the session and tell the teacher, who should be experienced with meditation-related difficulties, if that happens, and people with ringing in the ears may want to try it only briefly at first. Anyone with a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation should talk to a clinician before starting; it is untested.
modalities.tweet: No melody, no beat, no lyrics. One imagined note, held at the same pitch for 20 minutes like a quiet hum in your chest, as your only anchor. One Note, No Song is an untested idea for sound lovers who find silent breath practice too dry.

modalities.name: Not Even a Fidget
modalities.tagline: Let every urge to move pass by while you stay still.
modalities.whatItIs: Not Even a Fidget is a proposed solitary concentration practice in which the body expresses nothing at all for a set time: no swaying, no fidgeting and no change of expression. Where dancing turns feelings and impulses into movement shared with others, this lets each impulse to move pass unanswered, so that a deepening stillness becomes the object of attention.
modalities.coreIdea: Every urge to move is a small push toward expression or release, and letting those urges pass without acting on them, one after another, is meant to gather the mind into a calm that does not need to show itself.
modalities.whatYouDo: After a few lessons with a teacher, you choose a posture you can hold comfortably, seated with back support or lying down, and set a timer for 15 minutes at first, building to 30 over the weeks. Whenever an urge comes to scratch, shift, sway or open your eyes, you let it be there without acting on it or studying it, and return attention to the overall stillness of the body. If an urge stays strong or anything starts to hurt, you move slowly, settle again and carry on, because comfort matters more than a perfect score.
modalities.whoItsFor: Restless people who fidget through every quiet moment, and dancers or performers curious about the opposite of expression.
modalities.cautions: Never stay still through pain, numbness or a need to change position, and get up slowly afterward to avoid stiffness or dizziness. Deep stillness practice can bring up unusual or frightening experiences, so learn with a teacher experienced in meditation-related difficulties, and talk to a clinician first if you have a history of psychosis, bipolar disorder, severe trauma or dissociation; it is untested.
modalities.tweet: An itch, an urge to shift, a pull to sway: in this new concept you let each one pass without moving and rest in the stillness that builds. Start with 15 minutes, and never stay still through pain. The quiet opposite of a dance floor.
